help.intro: A text of about 200 words about the day the first railway in Germany ran: 7 December 1835, from Nürnberg to Fürth, six kilometres in nine minutes, with a locomotive called Adler that came from England together with its driver, who earned more than the mayor. The text tells what people feared, who rode along, and what became of the little railway. All facts are real and were checked. You read it in the past, the way Germans tell stories: Perfekt with haben for most verbs (hat gebaut, hat gekostet, haben gewartet) and with sein for movement and change (ist gefahren, ist gekommen, sind eingestiegen, ist geblieben). Read for the story first, then find one date, number or person per question.
help.tips[0].title: Perfekt with sein: movement and change
help.tips[0].text: sein + participle for verbs of movement from A to B (fahren, kommen, gehen, fliegen, laufen, einsteigen, ankommen) and for change of state (werden, aufstehen, einschlafen, sterben), plus sein and bleiben themselves: Der Zug ist gefahren. Die Lokomotive ist aus England gekommen. Die Leute sind eingestiegen. Alles ist gut geblieben. Everything else takes haben: Der Zug hat neun Minuten gebraucht. Die Leute haben Angst gehabt.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: The Adler ran for the first time on 7 December 1835 and arrived in Fürth after nine minutes.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: Two hundred people got on, and nobody fell ill.
help.tips[0].check.why: kommen is movement from A to B: sein + gekommen.
help.tips[1].title: Irregular participles in this text
help.tips[1].text: fahren → gefahren, kommen → gekommen, bleiben → geblieben, werden → geworden, steigen → gestiegen (eingestiegen), sehen → gesehen, bringen → gebracht, denken → gedacht, haben → gehabt, sein → gewesen. Separable verbs put ge- in the middle: ein-ge-stiegen, an-ge-kommen. Verbs on -ieren have no ge-: transportiert, passiert.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: Many people thought: that is dangerous! But nothing happened.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: The locomotive was brought to Nürnberg in parts.
help.tips[1].check.why: Separable verb: prefix + ge + stem: ein-ge-stiegen.
help.remember[0]: sein for movement and change: ist gefahren, gekommen, angekommen, geworden, geblieben.
help.remember[1]: haben for the rest: hat gebaut, gekostet, gedauert; -ieren without ge-: passiert.
help.exam: Short historical texts told in the Perfekt with dates and numbers are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: Six kilometres in nine minutes, a locomotive from England and a driver who earned more than the mayor: read about the first train in Germany.
passageTranslation:
On 7 December 1835 something new happened in Nürnberg: the first railway in Germany ran. The line was only six kilometres long, from Nürnberg to Fürth. The journey took nine minutes. By carriage people had needed over an hour before.

The locomotive was given the name Adler, eagle. It came from England, from the Stephenson company in Newcastle. It was brought to Nürnberg in parts by ship and horse cart. The driver came from England too: William Wilson. He earned 1,500 guilders a year, more than the mayor! He worked twenty years in Nürnberg and never went back to England.

Many people were afraid. Doctors said: at 35 kilometres per hour you get ill! The cows stop giving milk! But on 7 December two hundred people got on, music played, and everything went well. Nobody fell ill.

The little railway made money. In the first year 450,000 people rode along. But it did not transport only people: the first freight in the history of German railways was two barrels of beer.

The Adler ran until 1857. Then it was sold. Today a replica stands in the transport museum in Nürnberg. It still runs, on special days, slowly and with a lot of smoke.

questions[0].questionTranslation: How long was the first line, and how long did the journey take?
questions[1].explanation: "Sie ist aus England gekommen, von der Firma Stephenson in Newcastle."
questions[1].questionTranslation: Where did the locomotive come from?
questions[2].options[0]: weil kommen eine Bewegung von A nach B ist
questions[2].explanation: Verbs of movement from one place to another take sein in the Perfekt: ist gekommen.
questions[2].questionTranslation: 'It came from England.' Why ist and not hat?
questions[2].optionsTranslation[0]: because kommen is movement from A to B
questions[2].optionsTranslation[1]: because the locomotive is feminine and feminine nouns take sein in the perfect
questions[3].options[2]: Er ist nach einem Jahr mit der Lokomotive nach England zurückgefahren und nie wiedergekommen.
questions[3].explanation: "Er hat 1.500 Gulden im Jahr verdient, mehr als der Bürgermeister! Er hat zwanzig Jahre in Nürnberg gearbeitet und ist nie nach England zurückgefahren."
questions[3].questionTranslation: What is correct about William Wilson?
questions[3].optionsTranslation[0]: He was the mayor of Nürnberg.
questions[3].optionsTranslation[1]: He earned more than the mayor and stayed twenty years.
questions[3].optionsTranslation[2]: He went back to England with the locomotive after one year and never returned.
questions[4].explanation: "Ärzte haben gesagt: Bei 35 Kilometern pro Stunde wird man krank! Die Kühe geben keine Milch mehr!"
questions[4].optionsTranslation[1]: At 35 kilometres per hour you get ill.
questions[4].optionsTranslation[2]: The railway is good for health, especially for old people and children.
questions[5].explanation: "Die erste Fracht in der Geschichte der deutschen Eisenbahn waren zwei Fässer Bier."
questions[5].questionTranslation: What was the first freight of the German railways?
questions[6].explanation: "Im ersten Jahr sind 450.000 Menschen mitgefahren." Two hundred rode on the first day.
questions[6].questionTranslation: How many people rode along in the first year?
questions[7].explanation: "Heute steht ein Nachbau im Verkehrsmuseum in Nürnberg. Er fährt noch, an besonderen Tagen …"
questions[7].questionTranslation: Where can you see the Adler today?
questions[7].optionsTranslation[1]: as a replica in the transport museum in Nürnberg
questions[7].optionsTranslation[2]: at the station in Fürth, where it runs for tourists every Sunday
